item.title: Mapping Individual Brain Deviations in ICD-11 Catatonia: Normative Modeling of Structural and Functional MRI Across Two Independent Cohorts.
item.description:
The American journal of psychiatry
Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome cutting across mood disorders (MODs) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs). However, its neurobiological profiles remain poorly characterized. The authors examined structural and resting-state functional normative deviations associated with catatonia across two independent clinical cohorts, using hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling. Structural and resting-state functional MRI data were analyzed from two independent deeply phenotyped cohorts of 280 patients with MODs and SSDs. The Mannheim (Germany) sample included 184 patients with MODs or SSDs (58 with ICD-11 catatonia), and the Bern (Switzerland) sample comprised 96 SSD patients (59 with ICD-11 catatonia). Individual deviations from normative models were estimated using the PCNToolkit, based on healthy reference datasets (N=57,000 structural; N=22,000 functional). Catatonia diagnosis was associated with significant ventricular enlargement (third ventricle and left and right lateral ventricles; q<0.05) and cortical thinning in the left dorsal posterior cingulate and insular cortices (q<0.05) across both cohorts. Exploratory analyses identified a significant left orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) difference between MOD and SSD patients with catatonia. In the overall catatonia versus non-catatonia comparison, the OFC association survived false discovery rate correction only in models adjusted for demographic variables. Resting-state functional analyses showed reduced connectivity between sensorimotor, salience, limbic, and executive control networks at the nominal significance level, but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. In the combined sample, catatonia was characterized by ventricular enlargement and cingulo-insular cortical thinning, supporting a transdiagnostic model implicating distributed motor-salience integration circuits. These findings provide reproducible, individual-level evidence for distributed brain network involvement in catatonia and identify candidate regions for future mechanistic and neuromodulation studies.

item.title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

item.title: A Dynamic Model of Amygdala Circuits in Threat and Reward: Implications for Affective Disorders.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Animals must continuously evaluate their surroundings and select adaptive responses to survive in ever-changing environments. Central to this capacity is the assignment of importance to environmental cues, which guides motivated behavior toward rewarding opportunities and away from potential threats. Here we propose a theoretical framework, a dynamic motivational model based on threat and reward imminence, in which motivational states evolve continuously as a function of imminence rather than shifting between discrete stages. Within this framework, three interacting dimensions define the stimulus relevance of an environmental cue: salience, valence, and value. We leverage the amygdala as a substrate to illustrate the circuit mechanisms underlying importance assignment and examine how stimulus imminence drives motivational state transitions to promote adaptive behavior. Applied to affective disorders, it reframes amygdala dysfunction as projection- and circuit-specific stress adaptation rather than uniform regional hyperactivity, providing a common language for comparing major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders. By integrating animal circuit studies with human neuroimaging and clinical evidence, this framework positions amygdala-centered networks as candidate biomarkers for biologically informed subtyping and targets for personalized treatment in depression and related affective disorders.

item.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

item.title: Diagnostic and sex effects on frontostriatal brain wiring structural organization in early psychosis affective subjects compared to healthy controls.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Background Brain connectivity abnormalities may underlie affective psychosis which may be influenced by sex. Using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography, we assessed frontostriatal brain wiring connectivity patterns in 46 early psychosis affective and 56 healthy control young adult, male and female participants. Methods We collected harmonized whole brain tractography dMRI data from three sites and applied our novel fiber clustering methodology to identify 17 white matter fiber clusters connecting the frontal cortex and caudate per hemisphere in each group. By comparing cortical and caudate inter-cluster endpoint distances between groups, we assessed their patterns of frontostriatal connectivity. Results 1) In both males and females in early affective psychosis and healthy controls, bilaterally, the frontal cortex to caudate wiring pattern deviated from a topographic organization. 2) in a right hemisphere frontal pole fiber cluster, independent of sex, we found a significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.013); 3) in a left hemisphere inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, fiber cluster, we found sex influenced the significant interaction effect of diagnosis on the connectivity pattern between frontal cortex and caudate, (p = 0.0085), with the effect much greater in females (p < 0.00001) than in males (p = 0.97); and, 4) post-hoc tests showed a significant effect of diagnosis on the pattern of frontal cortex to caudate connectivity in specific subregions (ps ≤0.04). Conclusions Importantly, while the frontostriatal wiring pattern in both early affective psychosis and healthy controls deviated from a topographic organization, we found in a right hemisphere fiber cluster, independent of sex, that a significant interaction effect of diagnosis was observed on the frontal cortex to caudate connectivity pattern, whereas, in a left hemisphere fiber cluster, the effect of diagnosis on connectivity pattern was influenced by sex, showing the importance of the role of sex in brain wiring patterns in early affective psychosis.

item.title: SPARK-ICA: Guided Frequency-Resolved Dynamic Spatial ICA Reveals Fine-Scale fMRI Network Dynamics.
item.description:
Human brain mapping
Fine-scale spatiotemporal dynamics of functional brain networks are increasingly recognized as critical markers of transient connectivity and neuropsychiatric pathology. However, many existing dynamic fMRI methods primarily focus on temporal variability without explicitly resolving the spatial-frequency content of network dynamics, potentially limiting characterization of subtle, high-frequency spatial reconfigurations. To address this gap, we propose SPARK-ICA (Spatial-frequency Partitioned, Adaptive Reconstruction using Knowledge-guided ICA), a frequency-resolved dynamic spatial independent component analysis (ICA) framework that integrates NeuroMark template guidance with spatial frequency decomposition and group-level ICA of time-resolved, band-specific spatial maps. Starting from template-guided NeuroMark networks, we first estimate time-varying spatial maps using a dynamic guided ICA approach, capturing subject-specific network expression over time. Each dynamic spatial map is then decomposed into multiple spatial frequency bands using Fourier-domain spatial filtering, isolating fine- to coarse-scale spatial features at each time point. Band-specific spatial maps are subsequently concatenated and subjected to a blind group-level multi-frequency ICA, yielding a compact latent representation in which each dynamic component is characterized by distinct spatial-frequency signatures. These group-level band-resolved components are then used as references to estimate subject- and band-specific time courses and maps via spatially constrained ICA, enabling frequency-specific analysis of both long-term correlations and short-term temporal variability while preserving reproducibility across subjects. Using resting-state fMRI data from schizophrenia (SZ) patients and healthy controls (HC), we evaluated both long-term correlations and short-term variability of band-resolved dynamic time courses. For the group-level analyses, we focused on a predefined subset of NeuroMark networks with well-established involvement in SZ-related dysconnectivity. Our results reveal frequency-specific abnormalities in SZ, with enhanced long-term connectivity within sensory and subcortical networks and pronounced short-term alterations involving predominantly higher-frequency spatial components, particularly in cerebellar and subcortical systems. These findings indicate that SZ-related dysregulation is differentially expressed across spatial-frequency and temporal scales, rather than reflecting uniform dysconnectivity. Together, this framework provides a unified approach for analyzing dynamic fMRI networks across spatial, temporal, and frequency dimensions, extending our previous NeuroMark-DyFICA framework from a predominantly high-frequency spatial representation to an explicitly frequency-resolved characterization of dynamic network organization. By explicitly modeling spatial frequency-dependent dynamics, the proposed method provides a more resolved characterization of network alterations and offers a framework for identifying candidate markers of neuropsychiatric disorders.

item.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

item.title: Brain systems supporting the narrative self and psychopathology.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Disturbances in the narrative self are implicated across psychiatric disorders, with abnormalities in the neural systems supporting its generation and regulation constituting a transdiagnostic risk factor for mental illness. This review highlights how alterations in these brain systems underlie prevalent clinical features, including diminished, rigid, and sustained negative beliefs within the narrative self. The narrative self is framed as a higher-order construct that emerges from multiple systems, with reward, punishment, and motivational signals biasing which experiences are encoded as self-defining and which self-beliefs are reinforced over time. We discuss recent evidence demonstrating how the narrative self is supported by distributed brain networks in which subcortical inputs from the basal forebrain, habenula and mediodorsal thalamus modulate default mode network activity, with the salience, frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, and hippocampal-parahippocampal networks regulating how self-beliefs are established or updated. Adolescence is emphasized as a developmental period uniquely vulnerable to disturbances in the formation of a coherent, flexible narrative self, wherein asynchronous subcortical and cortical development and pubertal changes interact to confer risk for diminished and rigid self-beliefs. Belief-updating tasks, hierarchical computational models, and ecological momentary assessment are proposed as approaches to quantify how self-beliefs form and shift across time, linking neural signatures of the narrative self to momentary variability. We propose that treating the narrative self as a primary level of explanation for psychopathology positions it as a testable target for future neuroimaging research, providing a clearer bridge from self-referential cognition to interventions in daily life.
